newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Tide rising for rate changes - Belgian bond traders.
newsitem.headline: Tide rising for rate changes - Belgian bond traders.

text.p: Sentiment on the Belgian capital market has turned now that players are coming round to the view that German interest rates are on the way up, ending a prolonged spell in which key rates were at historically low levels.

The Belgian discount rate hit the low of the current cycle when it was slashed by half a percentage point in April 1996. The central rate -- a key indicator for overnight rates -- was lowered four months later to 3.00 percent from 3.20 percent.
Since then the National Bank has left the rate, closely tied to the Bundesbank's repo rate which is also at three percent, unchanged. Change is clearly on its way now, dealers said.
"Bit by bit people are starting to think of higher rates," a trader said.

Thursday's U.S. data, including July inflation, were on the whole benign for bond markets US-ECI, but the Federal Reserve was only waiting for confirmation of the strong fundamentals before moving rates higher in the autumn, he said.

The German Bundesbank was an unknown quantity when it came to the chances of a rate rise. But with German inflation at 1.9 percent -- uncomfortably close to the central bank's reference rate of two percent -- and the German economy poised for a recovery, rates could only go one way -- up, he added.
Analysts said the latest U.S. data provided markets with some relief, but would only allow some consolidation.
"I can see a slight recovery for the long end, maybe five to 10 basis points off," one said. "In the longer term the trend will turn and we will move closer to six percent," he added.
The benchmark 10-year OLO BE286= yielded 5.76 percent at 1410 GMT, down slightly from 5.79 late Wednesday.

Analysts said that whatever readings near-term releases of economic indicators might show, interest rate cycles had bottomed out, meaning the short end of yield curves was "out". The fate of the longer end depended on inflation trends.

Flattening trades were favoured. "There are still people out there looking to sell short and buy long," a trader said. ABN AMRO said, "We advise to take advantage of every serious steepening to put flatteners on."

One analyst said, "the Belgian economy is particularly sensitive to the prospects of a turnaround in the European interest rate cycle with its high levels of public debt...this would mainly affect the short end. At the long end fundamentals are pretty sound with the inflation outlook subdued."
He recommended short positions in marks, longs in European periferals, or better still longs in dollars.
One trader said, "Next week there will be a consolidation phase since there are few U.S. data and the only German statistics only indirectly reflect inflation pressures."
Another said, "I am positive for the short term, but we will soon get close to profit-taking levels...fundamentally, gains would be O.K. but I am careful at these levels."
